# Conventions: entities, type paths, and argument shapes

How to form the arguments every `brp` leaf expects. Read this once; the
per-command flag lists live in `reference/<group>.md`, and end-to-end
walkthroughs live in `reference/recipes.md`.

## Entity ids

- Entities are addressed by numeric id (u64), always as a positional:
  `bevy_copilot brp world get-components 4294967299 --components my_game::Health`.
- Get ids from `brp world query` results or from the `entity` field of a
  spawn / watch result.
- Replay remaps recorded spawn IDs to new IDs, and checkpoint restore spawns
  fresh entities and reports an `entity_map` (recorded ID -> new ID). Restore
  does not remove existing entities or reset the world: originals may still
  exist with their original IDs. Use the map when addressing restored copies.

## Type paths

- Components, resources, events, and messages are named by fully-qualified
  Rust type path: `my_game::Health`,
  `bevy_transform::components::transform::Transform`.
- Only reflect-registered types are visible over BRP. The app opts types in
  with `.register_type::<T>()`; an unregistered type does not exist as far
  as these commands are concerned.
- Discover what the app actually exposes instead of guessing:
  - `brp world list-components` — every component type path in the world
    (`--entity <ID>` scopes to one entity);
  - `brp world list-resources` — every resource type path;
  - `brp registry schema` — the full type registry with field shapes
    (large; narrow it with `--with-crates my_game` or `--type-limit <N>`).

## Query payloads (`brp world query`)

`--data` selects which components come back; `--filter` restricts which
entities match. Both are JSON objects:

- `--data '{"components": ["my_game::Health"]}'` — required components;
- add `"option": ["my_game::Mana"]` to also fetch components an entity may
  lack (missing ones are simply absent from the row, not an error);
- `--filter '{"with": ["my_game::Player"], "without": ["my_game::Dead"]}'`.

A required component filters out entities that lack it, regardless of `strict`.
Use `option` for may-have components. `--strict true` reports invalid component
types/reflection failures instead of tolerating them.

## Value payloads

- Component/resource maps are JSON objects keyed by type path:
  `--components '{"my_game::Health": {"value": 100.0}}'` (spawn, insert).
- Mutation uses a Bevy reflection path (fields, tuple indices, `[array indices]`,
  or an empty path for the whole value):
  `--component my_game::Health --path value --value 42.0`; nested fields work
  the same way (`--path translation.x`).
- Match the JSON shape and range to the Rust field type; examples use `100.0`
  for an `f32` field and `100` for a `u32` field. The reflected deserializer
  determines which numeric conversions are accepted.
- NaN and infinite floats cannot cross the wire: they arrive as `null`
  (JSON cannot represent them).

## Flag mechanics

- The call's main subject is positional (entity id, resource / event /
  message type path, schedule label, RPC method); everything else is a
  `--flag`.
- Booleans take explicit values: `--strict true`, `--skip-first false`.
- String lists are comma-delimited:
  `--components my_game::Health,my_game::Mana`.
- JSON flags must be valid JSON. In POSIX shells wrap them in single
  quotes so `"`, `$`, and spaces survive.
- `--host`, `--port`, `--compact` are global and parse anywhere in the
  command line; use per-call `--port` to pick among several running apps.

## Debug list arguments

`--setup '[{"method":"world.query","params":{"data":{"components":[]}}}]'`
accepts a complete JSON array; `--setup '[]'` is empty. Repeating `--setup`
with one object per occurrence is also supported. `--rules` accepts arrays or
repeatable objects in the same way. MCP uses JSON arrays directly.

Anomaly rules query component presence independently of selected values. Use
full type paths for `with` and `requires`; short names must resolve uniquely.
NL queries require full registered type paths in the query sent to BRP.
